taxonomy.subtopic: Preload-dependent left ventricular outflow tract obstruction

questions.stem_html: A 19-year-old competitive runner has exertional presyncope and a family history of sudden death. A harsh systolic murmur is heard along the left sternal border. The accompanying chart shows how the murmur changes with bedside maneuvers. Why does it become louder during the strain phase of the Valsalva maneuver?

options.text_html: Pulmonary venous congestion increases left atrial pressure and transmitral flow
Increased venous return enlarges the left ventricular cavity and accelerates flow across a fixed valve lesion
Increased systemic vascular resistance increases the pressure gradient across the dynamic obstruction
Reduced myocardial contractility prolongs ejection through the narrowed outflow tract
Reduced venous return decreases left ventricular cavity size, increasing systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve and dynamic outflow obstruction

questions.explanation_html: The strain phase of Valsalva decreases venous return and left ventricular end-diastolic volume. The smaller cavity brings the hypertrophied septum and anterior mitral leaflet closer together, increasing systolic anterior motion and the dynamic outflow gradient. Maneuvers that increase preload or afterload generally reduce this obstruction.

wrong_choice_explanations.2: Valsalva decreases rather than increases venous return.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Increased afterload tends to reduce the dynamic gradient by keeping the cavity larger during systole.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Lower contractility would reduce dynamic obstruction and murmur intensity.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: The change occurs through ventricular loading conditions, not an acute rise in pulmonary venous pressure.

questions.educational_objective: Dynamic obstruction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy worsens when preload falls because the smaller ventricular cavity promotes systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve.
